entry.title: The End of a First Attempt
entry.content:
The last day of the first regional competition in Bucharest had dawned. A long awakening, a hearty breakfast and watching Romanian electricians at work were followed by the journey to the venue of our last matches of this season. Laughter at travellers’ jokes was followed by a warm-up in the form of minor repairs to the robot and to the program itself. Fairly soon a volunteer called at our table to remind us to queue for our match. This time we approached the playing field alongside team Evolution (#19131), on the side of the red alliance. With a strategy forged the day before, we went into match number 96 at the sound of the horn. This time we felt extra tension, as we were up against our friends from team CSH (#17861). Despite our strategy and coordinated cooperation, we were simply a little slower than the opposing colour, and at the final whistle we were a few points short.

The members of the drive team returned to the table content and motivated. There was quite some time left until the next match, so we decided to visit colleagues and make new acquaintances. We made friends with team RoSofija. A discussion about the robot and the program grew into a fine friendship. They also gave us the Romanian version of Jaffa Cakes, which made a pleasant snack. Later in the event they called at our table again and talked with us about the present state of their country and its history. We became closest to two of their members, Frumo and Sebi.

Soon lunch was over too, and with it the time until our last qualification match, number 115. Still with the red square fixed to the side of the robot, we worked out a strategy in good time with team Gentlemen (#17857). For the last time, we pinned our Driver and Coach badges to our shirts and made our way to the playing field. The starting siren soon sounded, followed by a successful autonomous phase for both red teams. Whilst the spectators chanted ‘Haj rošu’ (‘Come on, red’), we manoeuvred about the field as efficiently as we possibly could and stuck to the agreed ‘circuit’ strategy. With a successfully completed circuit and a satisfying number of points, we managed to end our appearance at the FIRST Tech Challenge competition in a good light.

Soon after our last match, the alliance selection for the competition’s semi-finals began. More and more people gathered round the playing fields, on the balconies and on the stairs, so as to follow the semi-finals and finals live, even if by looking at the big screen. The tension and noise only mounted, adding to the atmosphere of the matches themselves, which were played on the principle of ‘the first team to win two matches wins’ (best of three).

When the noise of the audience and the horns had died away, we moved to the neighbouring pavilion, where the awards ceremony took place. The event involved a language foreign to us (without subtitles), applause, and cheering for our friends whenever they won an award. After the pleasant event, we met our friend Christian one last time at this event and managed to exchange a few more words.

We quickly worked out what came next on the programme for hungry and tired competitors – what else but dinner! After a short visit to our hotel rooms, we set off for the Carrefour Express shopping centre we already knew. Whilst we were choosing between fast-food outlets, our friends from teams DarkEnergy and DecebalTech came up to us. The conversation turned to less competitive topics, chiefly food and the city centre. A long conversation was followed by an even longer farewell, which nevertheless ended with plenty of smiles. In the end the great majority of us decided on the ChopStix restaurant, apart from a few who opted for Popeye’s. With full stomachs and goodies for the road, we made for the nearest underground station.

Thanks to a simple system and timetable, we were soon able to sit down on a train, which, in just a few minutes and in exchange for a good half a euro, took us to the city centre, close to the sight at the top of our list – the Parliament. On the way up to the surface we also encountered a simulation of the Karst – or rather of its famous bora wind. A few minutes’ walk brought us to the second-largest parliament building in the world, which we could view from a car park at a suitable distance from the front of the building.

We continued our tour of the city towards the old town centre, adorned with tall buildings, suspiciously dark underpasses and well-nigh unsolvable Kirchhoff loops. Fortunately the narrow streets had many small maps to help with orientation, so we could see sights such as the National Museum without difficulty. Owing to transport constraints we had to hurry, and on the way we could catch only a few closed shops, a church, the National Museum of Art, University Square and the statue of a seated man (Iuliu Maniu). Quick feet brought us to the station by the river in time, and then the train took us back to the neighbourhood of the Carrefour shopping centre.

The warmth of our hotel rooms put us in a state of comfort and encouraged one last evening get-together in Romania, which, alas, was partly taken up with packing tools and local energy drinks. Soon it was time for sleep, though for some sooner than for others. The new morning brought new adventures with it. As our flight was in the afternoon, we decided that after meeting two volunteers and swapping shirts, we would visit a sight close by – the lake Lacul Morii. After breakfast and handing in our key cards and luggage, we set off to see it. Our route led through a park which, together with its surroundings, had been worn by time and put us in mind of the Soviet style. The playground equipment and the goings-on were, despite the very pleasant sunny weather, rather uninspiring, if one does not count the military equipment on display in the park. The lake itself, however, is considerably larger than the park, and is surrounded by a running track and arches in a modern-art style, which served as a speed test with the help of pigeons. At the far end one could make out a small peninsula bearing the remains of ancient columns.

Soon we returned to the hotel, where all that remained was to wait for the Uber we had ordered and for a call from Sin Valentin. The ride to the airport offered us another taste of Romanian driving skills, as well as a look at sights such as the Triumphal Arch (Arcul de Triumf) and the Village Museum. Meeting up at the airport was followed by waiting, check-in and an explanation that the robot’s box did not, after all, contain bottles of wine. During the journey we also published a thank-you video for our supporters on this occasion, Zavarovalnica Triglav.

Until next time,
salut

entry.title: The Colours of Friendship
entry.content:
With a view of the rising sun, the nearby blocks of flats and a church, we began the second morning of our visit to Bucharest. A hearty breakfast was followed by a walk to the hall that was the main purpose of our journey. Instead of stretching exercises, we set about repairs to the robot and cracked our knuckles by hammering at keyboards. Adapting the gamepad’s button settings to the driver’s wishes and building the robot’s autonomous routine kept the programming part of the team busy until inspections and qualification matches began. The robot inspection was followed by the defence of yesterday’s written work, seasoned with the surname of one of Slovenia’s biathletes and the partial disintegration of the robot itself. After that we also had the robot’s performance tested on the playing field, where the autonomous part let us down. With minor repairs we passed the test and turned our attention to the next challenges, despite the ban on modifying the robot. Luck was on our side and moved our first match to the second day, which allowed us to make repairs. The robot’s operation was stabilised and the lifting mechanism improved to meet our requirements. Our drive team – David T. (driver), Ana (co-driver) and David Z. (coach) – attended a meeting on the first day intended to clear up any uncertainties and go over the rules again. The team captain, David T., also went over to our partners on the blue side in good time to discuss the game strategy that our pair of robots would try to carry out.

Our first qualification match (number 16 on the list) was played in partnership with team CYB3RG0DS (#22998) and ended in victory for our alliance, 107 to 89. With a far better feel for the game itself (and for handling the robot), we returned to the rest of the team and immediately set about the necessary repairs, and soon afterwards about forging strategies anew.

In between there were rests and strolls, during which we members of team VegaMind met new people and struck up friendships. Our best friends were at first our very neighbours, team BrutForce (#22941). Whilst getting acquainted, we were surprised at the number of members in some teams, which reached as many as 17, not counting mentors. Colour, logos, gifts and little chats adorned the corridor leading from the building’s entrance to the centre of the action. Amongst the teams we met (and got to know) the world champions of the 2021/2022 FTC season – Delta Force. Their robot certainly stood out, working by means of a crane-like mechanism. We also became good friends with some members of team CSH, above all with their spokesperson, Cristie, the only one who would readily come over for a chat.

The hours passed ever faster, just as the robots on the fields moved ever faster. The second match of our FTC career had arrived (number 38), in which we again appeared on the blue side, but this time with team Bots’ Brain (#19081). Somewhat poorer coordination and bad luck brought us a mere 41 points, which was not enough for a win. Tired, we returned to our place and quietly hoped for the arrival of food, which, despite its dreadful taste, managed to fill us up for a while.

Whilst testing the robot, we got to know some members of team Decebal Tech. Their programmer, Matej, showed our coding crew some resources worth their weight in gold, namely Road Runner and an artificial intelligence program. The former is meant to make life easier for programmers who want the robot to follow a more demanding curve. The latter makes image recognition simpler, which is a central part of the game’s autonomous phase, as parking in the correct part of the field (depending on the image on the cone) earns us extra points. Along with the resources, we also learnt that most programmers at the event do not ‘reinvent the wheel’, as the competition in Romania is so well developed that the great majority of programming solutions are readily available online. After this programming enlightenment, we also met some colleagues of that team, namely team DarkEnergy (#19106), made up of students from the same school, but from lower years.

Free time passes quickest of all, and so before long a volunteer, Liviu, who later became our friend, came up to us and reminded us that we needed to queue for the next match (number 53). Still with the blue circle pinned to the side of our robot, we went into a new duel alongside our colleagues from team November Eleven (#21073). This time we suffered a worse slip-up: we could not control the robot. Because a sensor failed to trigger, the driver was denied access to the robot. All it needed was a tap on the head, but touching the robot during a match is strictly forbidden. Two agonising minutes dragged on, and sadly we could do nothing to help our colleagues. With a mere 42 points, we shook hands with our fellow blues and the reds alike and, with the motto ‘gracious professionalism’ in mind, marched back to those waiting for us. To say that the two programmers had their work cut out would be an understatement. Fortunately the problem was soon put right, which we also tested carefully on the field.

During the hectic day we received a visit from the Romanian version of the team’s favourite teacher – Christian! Full of positive energy and in somewhat simplified English, Christian greeted us and thanked us for coming. Sadly, as one of the chief organisers and judges, Christian was very busy and could not stay long, but we were glad of the visit. Now, back to work!

The last match of the second day of the FTC competition was drawing ever nearer. The match, recorded as number 70, was the last challenge before a well-earned rest. Exchanging the blue circle for a red square, we took our place beside the members of team HYPERCUBE (#20925). With a solid strategy and a calm approach, we listened to the loud (very loud) blasts of the sirens and the clamour of the crowd. The autonomous part of the program ran correctly. After 30 seconds the drivers seized their gamepads and set their sights on victory. The intended manoeuvres and a modest number of stacked cones turned the start of the match into a work of art. Whilst placing the fifth cone on a distant pole that blocked our view, we made a fatal error – the cone fell into the robot. As the game forbids carrying more than one cone at a time, we were forced to remove the cone from inside the robot, and our partners were unable to help us in time. For the rest of the match we tried to shake off our mistakes, but in vain, as the final whistle overtook us. The referee’s smile and respect were a sign to us that we should hold our heads high. The end of the exhausting day had come, but this time we decided to head back to the hotel before ten o’clock in the evening.

After a brief visit to our little rooms, we set off for the long-awaited shopping centre – AFI Cotroceni. We got there by a path through a park and by crossing the Romanian answer to Ljubljana’s Celovška cesta. A blue sphere and a growing number of people told us that we were not far from our destination. Famished, we first threw ourselves into the hunt for food – well, restaurants, to be precise. Just after discovering an ice rink, a zip line and a large number of restaurants all in one place, we found a machine that uses a robotic arm to make heart-shaped candyfloss on a stick. After lengthy deliberation over where to have a more serious meal, we chose NoodlePack, apart from the chicken lovers, who ended up in the queue for KFC.

Dinner was followed by a stroll through the building and a longer visit to a bookshop with board games and records. We rounded off our tour with a visit to a shop, where each of us treated ourselves to a few goodies in exchange for a few lions (that is, Romanian lei). The way back was filled with laughter, stumbling and the interpretation of modern art. Soon we were back at the hotel, but still far from the land of dreams.

Until next time,
ajaje

entry.title: Back to the Ibis!
entry.content:
Soon after returning home, the team took the decision to jump in at the deep end – we wished to take part in the FIRST Tech Challenge competition (FTC for short). We European teams are somewhat limited in qualifying tournaments, so our path led us to Bucharest, the capital of Romania. After plenty of sleepless nights and days spent debugging, we boarded an aeroplane that took us, with a stopover in Belgrade, to Bucharest. The city greeted us with taxi chaos, which was resolved by Uber and an air-conditioning repairman, Sin Valentin. A ride without seat belts, and a tour of half the city’s sights along the way, were followed by checking in at the Ibis hotel, a chain we had already made ourselves at home with during our visit to Geneva! In the lobby we already met a few of our fellow competitors. Owing to our rather late arrival and the untrustworthy look of the surroundings, we decided to spend our first night in Romania visiting the nearest shop and walking to the venue where the FTC competition would take place over the coming days.

The advantage of our lodgings’ location is that we wake up a 10-minute walk from the building of the Politehnica University of Bucharest, which stands on a student campus together with plenty of other engineering faculties. A 𝐹𝐼𝑅𝑆𝑇-coloured corridor and a crowd of lively fellow competitors hinted that we were in the right place. After a walk to the practice fields, which are located near the main competition fields and the stage, we also found, close by, the table – or rather the pit – of our team, VegaMind #22903. The look round was followed by changing the lettering on our Vegova clothes to VegaMind, which sticky tape made possible.

On our return to the largest of our three rooms, a heap of work awaited us in writing documentation, namely the written submissions, the ‘Engineering Notebook’ and the ‘Team Portfolio’. The practice of staying up into the small hours proved useful after all when playing a game of Exploding Kittens.

After a hearty breakfast, we finished our written work and, with a polite request, had it printed at the hotel reception. The morning had a working flavour, as access to the practice field let us refine our programming solutions. Besides these duties, we also set about repairs to the robot itself, on which we had discovered a few shortcomings. Test drives showed us the robot’s real capabilities, namely that we could aim only for the ground junctions and the lowest poles. We also attended the opening ceremony, which was in Romanian, admittedly, but we managed to contribute too, by donating a ‘shirt’ for the group photograph.

Besides engineering activities, the first day also brought social ones, as we made friends with some teams and looked at our fellow competitors’ robots, the sight of which brought sweat to our brows.

We rewarded our work into the small hours with a visit to the nearby Carrefour Orhideea shopping centre, where we treated ourselves to drinks we had never seen before and explored the world of Romanian snacks. The walk back to the hotel was followed by planning the new day and a pinch more work.

Until next time,
takle mamo
